title: Culture and Aesthetic Preference: Comparing the Attention to Context of East Asians and Americans

findings.consequent: Location of the horizon in landscape paintings (percentage of frame height)
findings.mechanism: East Asian perspective allows artists to use multiple viewpoints, placing the horizon higher to include more contextual information.
findings.quote: the location of the horizon in East Asian paintings was significantly higher than that of Western paintings, t(581) = 10.39, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Ratio of the face area to the entire visual field in portraits (percentage)
findings.mechanism: East Asian painters deemphasize the face in portraits, consistent with contextual emphasis.
findings.quote: the ratio of the size of the face to the size of the entire visual field was substantially smaller in East Asian than in Western portraits, t(415) = 9.10, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Location of the horizon in paintings of people in a scene (percentage of frame height)
findings.mechanism: East Asian paintings are more likely than Western paintings to depict field information.
findings.quote: the location of the horizon was significantly higher in East Asian than in Western paintings, t(399) = 6.08, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Ratio of the largest face area to the entire visual field in paintings of people in a scene (percentage)
findings.mechanism: East Asian paintings emphasize contextual information over the figure.
findings.quote: The ratio of the size of the largest face to the size of the entire visual field was significantly smaller in East Asian than in Western paintings, t(399) = 2.88, p < .005.

findings.consequent: Average location of horizons drawn in landscape pictures (percentage of picture plane)
findings.mechanism: People maintain culturally specific ways of drawing, reflecting context-inclusive styles.
findings.quote: the average location of horizons drawn by East Asians was 19% higher in the picture plane than those drawn by Americans, t(87) = 2.98, p < .005.

findings.consequent: Number of additional contextual objects drawn in landscape pictures
findings.mechanism: East Asians drew 74% more contextual objects, indicating greater context inclusiveness.
findings.quote: East Asians drew 74% more contextual objects than did Americans, t(87) = 2.16, p < .05.

findings.consequent: Size of faces in portrait photographs taken by participants (percentage of frame)
findings.mechanism: East Asians tended to place the model in the background, whereas Americans prioritized the figure.
findings.quote: there was a main effect of culture, F(1, 76) = 6.77, p < .02.

findings.consequent: Self-reported preference for smaller models (9-point rating scale)
findings.mechanism: Japanese were more likely to prefer smaller models, consistent with context-inclusive aesthetics.
findings.quote: the Japanese (M = 3.70) were more likely than their Americans counterparts (M = 4.89) to prefer smaller models, t(99) = 3.20, p = .002.

findings.consequent: Self-reported preference for context-inclusive pictures (9-point rating scale)
findings.mechanism: Japanese were more likely to prefer context-inclusive images, reflecting holistic attention.
findings.quote: the Japanese (M = 3.79) were more likely than Americans (M = 4.57) to prefer context-inclusive pictures, t(99) = 1.99, p = .05.

findings.mechanism: Middle-range lenses (standard/narrow background) were generally preferred over extremely wide or extremely narrow backgrounds.
findings.quote: there was a main effect of lens, F(1, 98) = 12.05, p < .001.

findings.antecedent: Culture (American vs. Japanese) x Lens focal length (breadth of context)
findings.mechanism: Japanese rated extremely narrow backgrounds more negatively than Americans, showing cultural differences in context preference.
findings.quote: there was an interaction of culture and lenses, F(3, 98) = 7.04, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Average preference for background size (selection from sets with same model size)
findings.mechanism: Japanese were more likely to prefer wider width backgrounds, while Americans preferred context exclusive images.
findings.quote: there was only a main effect of culture, F(1, 98) = 7.90, p < .006. In general, the Japanese were more likely than Americans to prefer wider width backgrounds.

findings.mechanism: The 1.25-in. model was generally preferred by both groups of participants.
findings.quote: there was a main effect for the size of the model, F(1, 98) = 35.82, p < .001.

findings.antecedent: Culture (American vs. Japanese) x Model size
findings.mechanism: Japanese were less likely than Americans to prefer extremely large models (1.75-in. and 2.25-in.).
findings.quote: there was an interaction of culture and model, F(3, 98) = 7.04, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Average preference for model size (selection from sets with same background size)
findings.mechanism: Japanese were more likely than Americans to prefer small models.
findings.quote: there was a main effect of culture, F(1, 98) = 6.34, p < .013 (see Table 5). In general, the Japanese were more likely than the Americans to prefer small models.

stimuli.description: Digital images of traditional East Asian (660) and Western (731) landscape, portrait, and people-in-scene paintings (15th-19th centuries) from major museums.
Blank 8.5 x 11 inch paper with a black frame for participants to draw landscapes.
Digital camera (Sony Digital Mavica 500) used by participants to photograph confederates in various laboratory and atrium settings.
Sets of four artificially composed portrait photographs manipulated for background breadth (using 28mm, 50mm, 100mm, 140mm lenses) and model size (0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25 inches tall).

limitations: The study cannot isolate the exact cognitive-perceptual information processing that produced the reported results.
Identifying the causal directions among artistic traditions, perceptual habits, and preferred representations is beyond the scope of the current article.
Representational preferences might merely reflect adherence to artistic traditions rather than genuinely different ways of seeing the world, potentially lacking profound psychological meaning.
